entry.title: Building Redoubt Analytics: A Counter-UAS Risk Intelligence Platform
entry.summary: Airports, ports, data centers, and energy grids all share a growing vulnerability: low-cost, high-capability drones. A few years ago, a serious counter-UAS conversation was mostly a military one. Today it belongs on the desk of any Chief Security Officer responsible for a large physical site, because the barrier to entry for building or buying a capable drone has collapsed while the value of the assets sitting under our skies has only gone up. Unlike traditional physical security threats, Unmanned Aerial Systems (UAS) are cheap, fast-moving, and hard to model with conventional risk frameworks. A fence, a badge reader, and a guard rotation are all static countermeasures against a mostly static threat. A drone swarm is neither static nor predictable, and it doesn't respect a perimeter fence …

entry.title: Why I Built a Local-First Password Manager Instead of Another Cloud Vault
entry.summary: Most password managers solve the same problem the same way: encrypt locally, then ship a synced copy to their cloud. That model works. It’s also a huge blast radius. One vendor outage, one account takeover, one compliance surprise—and every device that trusts that sync plane is in the story. I wanted a different default: your vault lives on your devices. Sync is optional, and when you use it, it stays on your network—not a hosted vault backend you have to trust forever. That’s SafeVault (Password Safe Vault): a Flutter password manager with AES-256-GCM encryption, a security dashboard, and desktop workflows built for people who live in a keyboard. Cloud sync is convenient until it isn’t. Privacy-conscious users (and a lot of developers) don’t want a third party holding an encrypted blob of…

entry.title: Styling the dialog element: open is not the same as modal
entry.summary: The <dialog> element ships in a closed state. display: none by default, no visible box to style until you open it. That's the first thing that trips a hand-styled version: you're writing CSS for a component you can't see on the page yet. Two methods open it, and they do not behave the same. show() opens a non-modal dialog: no backdrop, the page behind stays interactive, Esc does not close it. showModal() opens a modal one: it gets a backdrop, centers itself, listens for Esc, and makes the rest of the page inert. The CSS-Tricks piece by Geoff Graham pulls those apart before touching a single style, because the styling hooks are different too. There are three ways to write "the dialog is open" in CSS, and they overlap without being interchangeable. [open] is the attribute selector. It matche…

Boards built around the RP2040 now sit at the center of homemade synths, MIDI pads, and touch instruments that would have cost hundreds a decade ago. entry.title: Mastering the Producer-Consumer Pattern in Java LLD: The Restaurant Kitchen
entry.summary:
Mastering the Producer-Consumer Pattern in Java LLD: The Restaurant Kitchen
The Producer-Consumer pattern is a staple in Java Machine Coding interviews because it tests your real-world concurrency control without breaking thread safety. Mastering it proves you can handle asynchronous thread handoffs without burning CPU cycles or risking deadlocks. Writing custom lock logic using wait() and notifyAll() inside synchronized blocks, introducing subtle race conditions and spurious wakeup bugs. Busy-waiting inside while(true) loops with non-thread-safe collections, thrashing the CPU while repeatedly checking queue sizes.
